description:
We are some space enthusiastic students with a motive to build an unique solution for the Mars Planet explorers to safely travel on the planet.

In our Team, We have Sauda Rahman (Team Lead & Storyteller), Sumaiya Akter Fabia (Visionary & UI/UX Designer), and Rafi Adnan (Full Stack Developer).
summary:
MARSWalk is a web tool that helps Mars astronauts plan safe science walks, built around the boxwork terrain on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. It lays Curiosity’s real drive history over NASA topographic and optical maps from Mars Trek, then colours the track by slope. Four boxwork science stops, such as the Altadena drill site, are placed on that track, and the crew can reorder them, add their own, and see rover photos from each location. The planner builds a multi-stop route and, if it doesn’t fit one spacewalk, splits it into several. For every leg it shows time, slope, sun angle, temperature and radiation dose. It also checks NASA’s DONKI feed for solar storms and runs a go/no-go safety checklist.

This answers NASA’s challenge for a layered, hyperlocal map that combines topographic, optical, slope, chemical, radiation and atmospheric data, with safety, crew mobility and point-of-view imagery. It matters because the first Mars crews will have no quick help from Earth, since messages can take up to twenty minutes, so they need to plan their own routes and judge risk themselves.
details:
MARSWalk is a web tool for planning science walks across the boxwork terrain on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. It loads Curiosity’s real drive history from NASA and draws it over NASA topographic and optical maps, colouring the track by slope. Four boxwork science stops are placed on that track by matching their sol numbers to the drive record. The crew can reorder the stops, add their own, choose a base camp, and pick solo, buddy-pair or rover-assisted travel. The planner builds out-and-back routes and splits them into several spacewalks if they don’t fit the time limit. For each leg it shows distance, time, slope, elevation change, sun angle, temperature and radiation dose. A go/no-go checklist, hazard protocols, a live solar-storm check and rover photos from each stop complete the safety picture.

Benefits

Crews get one hyperlocal view that combines terrain, slope, daylight, radiation and science targets, instead of switching between separate global tools. Because the routes follow ground a rover has already crossed, the mobility risk is lower. The app makes safety decisions quicker and clearer, which matters when messages from Earth can take up to twenty minutes.

Intended impact

We want to show how scattered NASA mission data can become a practical planning tool for the first human Marswalk. The same approach could be reused for other sites and adapted for a tablet or helmet display.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS and the Leaflet map library
  • A Node.js serverless function on Vercel that relays NASA requests
  • GitHub for version control and Vercel for hosting
  • NASA data: JPL MMGIS, Mars Trek, DONKI, the Mars Rover Photos API and the NASA Image Library
  • The Mars24 algorithm (Allison and McEwen, 2000) for the Mars clock and a Tobler hiking function for walking time
  • No special hardware: standard laptops and web browsers
  • AI assistance was used for code, scripts and the video voiceover. Check the Space Apps rules on disclosing AI use and state it if required.

How it is creative

We turned a rover’s drive history into a human-scale route by treating it as proven ground. Rover tilt becomes a slope measure, and the planner packs science stops into multiple EVAs automatically. Safety protocols react to live data. The tool also shows which values are live NASA data, which are embedded from publications and which are our own models, with a built-in connection test.

Factors we considered

  • Astronaut safety first: radiation, space weather, dust season, steep ground, cold and daylight
  • Mobility in a pressure suit while carrying equipment, and pair or rover-assisted work
  • Honesty about the data: live, embedded and modelled values are labelled, and the app shows an error instead of inventing positions
  • Reliability: fallbacks, a cached copy of the traverse and a connection test
  • Known limits: no obstacle detection yet, approximate sol placement of some stops, and coarse basemap resolution
